paragraphs: Distributed optimization spreads learning across multiple participants, making the interaction between local computation and shared information central to algorithm behavior. This paper studies those interactions through stochastic feedback control. Its main contribution is a common mathematical description that connects a substantial class of distributed learning algorithms to discrete-time control systems.

The framework accommodates multiple sampling rates, allowing different parts of an algorithm to operate on different schedules. The authors show that it covers Gradient Tracking for decentralized learning and FedPD and Scaffold for federated learning. Expressing these methods within the same framework makes it possible to analyze their convergence through a shared set of tools.

The framework also supports algorithm design under practical complications, including partial participation, compressed communication, and imperfect communication. The abstract further identifies differential privacy guarantees as a feature that can be incorporated. The significance is a reusable approach to analysis and design across the covered algorithm class, with control theory providing the organizing perspective.
icml-2022-a-stochastic-multi-rate-contro.tldr: A feedback-control framework unifies the modeling and convergence analysis of a substantial class of distributed optimization algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to build a controller by combining a supplied collection of controllers for an unknown environment. The learner can produce a new mixture rather than simply select one existing option. This is useful when controllers developed in simulations or different environments need to be adapted to a target setting with relatively few trials.

The authors propose a policy-gradient algorithm and a second algorithm that can use either an actor-critic or natural actor-critic scheme, depending on the available information. Both search within a class of mixtures of the supplied controllers. The policy-gradient convergence guarantees assume access to a gradient oracle; the actor-critic analysis guarantees convergence to a stationary point, while the natural actor-critic analysis reaches a global optimum.

Numerical studies examine inverted-pendulum stabilization and a constrained queueing task. They show that the proposed mixture optimization can stabilize a system even when the available base policies are unstable. This establishes a demonstrated benefit of combining controllers, without claiming that every collection of unstable controllers admits a successful mixture.
icml-2022-actor-critic-based-improper-re.tldr: Optimizing mixtures of existing controllers can produce stronger controllers, with convergence guarantees and demonstrated stabilization from unstable base policies.

paragraphs: Prediction intervals express uncertainty by giving a range around a forecast. Standard conformal prediction relies on exchangeability, an assumption that does not accommodate general time-series dependence. This paper investigates Adaptive Conformal Inference, or ACI, as a useful procedure for dependent time series beyond the distribution-shift setting that originally motivated it.

The authors theoretically examine how ACI’s learning rate affects efficiency in exchangeable and autoregressive cases. This matters because an adaptation procedure’s behavior depends on how quickly it responds to new observations. They then introduce AgACI, a parameter-free method that uses online expert aggregation to adaptively combine ACI procedures, addressing the choice of adaptation settings through aggregation.

Simulation comparisons support the use of ACI for time series, and an electricity-price forecasting study evaluates the proposed aggregation method in practice. AgACI produces efficient intervals for day-ahead forecasts in that study. Together, the theoretical analysis and empirical results support adaptive conformal methods for this setting, while keeping the theoretical conclusions tied to the cases actually analyzed.
icml-2022-adaptive-conformal-predictions.tldr: AgACI aggregates adaptive conformal procedures to produce time-series prediction intervals without manually selecting an adaptation parameter.

paragraphs: Predicting an information cascade’s popularity means estimating how many messages it will accumulate by a chosen future time. The paper approaches this through self-exciting Hawkes processes, which describe cascading activity in which events can stimulate further events. The goal is to support forecasts at different future horizons using the events already observed.

For general marked Hawkes point processes, the authors derive closed-form expressions for the conditional mean and variance of future event counts. These quantities describe the expected amount of future activity and its variability given the cascade’s history. The expressions provide a mathematical foundation for forecasting counts directly from an observed, partially developed cascade.

The authors use these results to construct CASPER, a regression approach specifically designed for popularity prediction. This distinguishes its predictive purpose from existing point-process approaches focused on generative modeling. Experiments with synthetic and real-world data report considerable accuracy improvements over prior work, especially early in a cascade, when the available observations are still limited.
icml-2022-anytime-information-cascade-po.tldr: CASPER uses conditional event-count formulas for Hawkes processes to improve cascade-popularity forecasts, particularly at early stages.

paragraphs: Collaboration of Experts combines several networks that specialize in different portions of a dataset. For each input, a delegator chooses an expert and also produces a rough prediction that can permit early termination. This connects the collective capacity of multiple networks with a mechanism for controlling how much computation an individual input requires.

Training coordinates the delegator and experts through two modules. The weight generation module solves a balanced transportation problem to partition training data according to the delegator, then reweights losses so each expert concentrates on its assigned portion. The label generation module supplies the training labels used to teach the delegator which expert to select.

On ImageNet, CoE reaches 80.7% top-1 accuracy with 194 million FLOPs. Combined with PWLU and CondConv, it reaches 80.0% with 100 million FLOPs. Translation experiments also support its applicability beyond image classification. The paper additionally reports hardware acceleration relative to existing conditional-computation approaches, connecting its computational savings to practical execution.
icml-2022-collaboration-of-experts-achie.tldr: CoE jointly trains specialized networks and a delegator, reaching 80.0% ImageNet top-1 accuracy at 100 million FLOPs when combined with PWLU and CondConv.

paragraphs: A growing document collection contains both changing subject matter and connections between documents. This paper develops two neural topic models that learn topic distributions using both sources of information. The aim is to represent how document content evolves while also accounting for the network in which those documents are linked.

The first model introduces Time-Aware Optimal Transport. It incorporates timestamps into a method that uses semantic distance to estimate the probability of a link between two documents from different times. This connects the topic representation to relationships across the document network, rather than treating temporal changes in individual documents as the only modeling target.

The second model adds a Temporal Point Process to represent how historical neighbors affect the formation of current links. It therefore also accounts for the influence of the network’s evolving structure. Experiments on four dynamic document networks show an advantage for the proposed models in jointly representing document dynamics and network adjacency, supporting the value of modeling content and connections together.
icml-2022-dynamic-topic-models-for-tempo.tldr: Two neural topic models combine changing document content with temporal links and network history to model evolving document networks.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning a threshold function from a crowd of annotators, some of whom may respond adversarially. The objective is PAC learning: obtaining a sufficiently accurate predictor with high probability. In this setting, the learner must manage unreliable responses while keeping both the annotation effort and computation efficient.

The central idea is to supplement direct label requests with pairwise comparisons, which the abstract describes as easier to acquire. The authors develop a comparison-assisted procedure that reliably recovers the true labels of a small group of examples. They then introduce a label-efficient filtering process that uses this small labeled group to infer true labels for a much larger collection.

The resulting approach can exponentially reduce the number of label queries while preserving overall query complexity and runtime. The distinction between labels and total queries is essential: the improvement concerns how much direct labeling is needed, while comparisons remain part of the information gathered. The result applies to the studied threshold-learning problem with potentially adversarial annotators.
icml-2022-efficient-pac-learning-from-th.tldr: Pairwise comparisons can exponentially reduce direct label requirements for crowdsourced threshold learning while preserving total query complexity and runtime.

paragraphs: Machine translation commonly uses separate encoder and decoder stacks for processing source and target text. This paper examines the alternative of a language model that processes concatenated sequences within one stack. It systematically varies architecture, model size, and data conditions across bilingual, multilingual, and zero-shot translation tasks.

The results show that language-model architectures scale differently. Design choices often strongly affect translation quality at smaller model sizes, while performance gaps narrow as parameter counts increase. The study also finds that causal masking and language-modeling objectives applied to the source sequence can hurt translation quality, highlighting the importance of how the source is processed.

With fully visible masking for the source sequence, language models can match encoder-decoder performance on supervised bilingual and multilingual translation. They also improve substantially on zero-shot translation directions by helping reduce outputs in the wrong target language. The findings make architectural details and source visibility central to interpreting comparisons between these model families, rather than treating every single-stack language model as equivalent.
icml-2022-examining-scaling-and-transfer.tldr: Translation experiments show that source-sequence visibility and model scale strongly influence whether single-stack language models match encoder-decoder systems.

paragraphs: A decision rule can affect both how fairly people are treated and how they change their reported features to obtain favorable outcomes. This paper studies these issues together. Its central question is how fairness policies and strategic manipulation influence one another when the people being evaluated respond to the algorithm.

The authors model the interaction as a two-stage Stackelberg game. The decision maker designs a rule while anticipating that individuals may manipulate their features. They analytically characterize equilibrium strategies for both sides, then examine how anticipating manipulation changes the resulting algorithm and its fairness properties. Fairness interventions are also analyzed through their effects on those equilibrium strategies.

The findings identify conditions under which anticipating strategic behavior can either reduce or worsen unfairness. They likewise identify conditions under which fairness interventions can encourage or discourage manipulation. The contribution is therefore conditional guidance about interacting incentives, rather than a claim that strategic awareness or fairness constraints always move outcomes in a beneficial direction.
icml-2022-fairness-interventions-as-dis-.tldr: A game-theoretic analysis identifies when fairness interventions encourage or discourage manipulation and when anticipating manipulation improves or worsens fairness.

paragraphs: Active learning chooses which unlabeled examples should receive labels, aiming to train an effective model with limited annotation. This becomes difficult in open-world settings where the classes of interest occupy only a small fraction of the data. Most examples may belong to an irrelevant or out-of-distribution class, creating extreme imbalance in the available pool.

GALAXY combines graph-based active learning with deep learning to address that imbalance. It adaptively selects examples that produce a more balanced labeled collection than most competing active-learning methods. The theoretical analysis describes the approach as a refined form of uncertainty sampling and shows that it gathers a substantially more class-balanced dataset than ordinary uncertainty sampling.

Experiments on imbalanced vision-classification settings constructed from popular datasets show advantages over existing leading deep active-learning algorithms. The practical contribution is a selection strategy that accounts for the difficulty of finding relevant classes within a heavily imbalanced pool. Its theoretical and empirical results connect better selection balance with effective learning in the studied settings.
icml-2022-galaxy-graph-based-active-lear.tldr: GALAXY uses graph-based selection to gather more class-balanced labels and improve active learning under extreme class imbalance.

paragraphs: Vision-language pretraining teaches a model to connect text with image content. Many existing methods use features extracted by object detectors and align those features with text. The paper identifies a difficulty with this object-centered approach: learning relationships involving multiple objects can be challenging when the representation is organized around individual detected objects.

X-VLM addresses this through alignments at multiple levels of granularity. Given associated text, the model learns to locate the corresponding visual concepts in an image while also aligning those concepts with the text. Localization and alignment therefore work together, giving pretraining a way to connect language with visual content at more than one level.

Experiments show that the learned alignments transfer effectively to multiple downstream vision-language tasks. X-VLM consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in the reported evaluation. The findings support multi-grained alignment as a useful pretraining strategy: matching text to visual concepts at different granularities provides representations that can serve several subsequent tasks, rather than being useful only for the pretraining exercise.
icml-2022-multi-grained-vision-language-.tldr: X-VLM jointly learns to locate visual concepts and align them with text at multiple granularities, improving downstream vision-language performance.

paragraphs: Approximating the self-attention matrix is one route to making Transformers more efficient. Existing approaches include predefined sparsity patterns, low-rank representations, and combinations of the two. This paper revisits multiresolution analysis, including ideas associated with wavelets, as another way to organize an approximation of the attention computation.

The central perspective is to represent attention at multiple resolutions. The authors develop their approximation using empirical feedback together with design decisions informed by modern hardware and implementation challenges. This makes the contribution a practical attention method as well as an application of classical mathematical ideas: the design considers how the approximation will actually be executed.

An extensive experimental evaluation finds that the resulting method outperforms most efficient self-attention proposals and performs favorably for both short and long sequences. These are comparative empirical findings, supporting a broad performance profile across the criteria considered. The short-sequence result also matters because the reported advantages are not confined to inputs with especially large sequence lengths.
icml-2022-multi-resolution-analysis-mra-.tldr: A hardware-informed multiresolution approximation of self-attention performs favorably against most efficient-attention alternatives on both short and long sequences.

paragraphs: Federated learning combines information from participants without collecting their raw data in one place. A central difficulty is that participants can have different data distributions, so their local learning signals may differ substantially. This paper proposes changing what participants communicate to make the shared information more expressive in that heterogeneous setting.

Participants upload sample-wise Jacobian matrices instead of model weights or gradients. These matrices describe how model outputs respond to parameter changes for individual samples. Using the neural tangent kernel framework, the server constructs an empirical kernel matrix and updates a global model without explicitly running gradient descent. The paper also develops a variant intended to improve communication efficiency and privacy.

Numerical experiments show that the proposed paradigm can reach the same accuracy as federated averaging with an order-of-magnitude reduction in communication rounds. This result concerns the number of rounds needed in the reported experiments. It supports the value of richer update information for coordinating learning across participants with different data distributions.
icml-2022-neural-tangent-kernel-empowere.tldr: Sharing sample-wise Jacobians enables kernel-based federated updates that experimentally match federated averaging accuracy with far fewer communication rounds.

paragraphs: Unconstrained online linear optimization studies sequential decisions without requiring a predefined bound on the comparator used to judge performance. Many algorithms use potential functions to guide their updates, but designing those functions often involves guesswork. This paper introduces a framework that generates potential functions by solving a partial differential equation.

For 1-Lipschitz losses, the framework yields an algorithm with an anytime regret guarantee. Its bound depends on the number of rounds, the size of an arbitrary comparator, and a user-chosen constant C. The comparator can be unknown and unbounded in advance. The guarantee achieves an optimal trade-off between loss and regret without relying on the doubling trick.

A matching lower bound establishes that the leading term is tight, including its square-root-of-two multiplier. This makes the contribution more precise than an improvement in the general growth rate of regret: the leading constant is also optimal within the stated setting. The PDE framework additionally supplies a systematic route to constructing the potential behind the algorithm.
icml-2022-pde-based-optimal-strategy-for.tldr: Solving a PDE yields a potential-based online-learning algorithm with an optimal anytime loss-regret trade-off for 1-Lipschitz losses.

paragraphs: Transformer pretraining often asks a model to reconstruct hidden input content. This paper explores a different task: infer where an input token belongs from its content, without supplying its positional information. To succeed, the model must learn relationships among the contents of different parts of the input that reveal their positions.

The task is implemented as classification over the possible positions for each token. This provides a simple training objective for learning positional relationships through content alone. It addresses the broader challenge of using Transformers’ representational capacity effectively, where sufficient data or strong regularization is needed to control overfitting.

Experiments on vision and speech benchmarks show improvements over strong supervised-training baselines and performance comparable to modern unsupervised or self-supervised pretraining methods. The method also enables Transformers without position embeddings to outperform models trained with full positional information in the reported experiments. These findings support position prediction as an effective pretraining signal, without establishing that explicit positional information is unnecessary in every Transformer application.
icml-2022-position-prediction-as-an-effe.tldr: Predicting token positions from content provides effective Transformer pretraining on vision and speech benchmarks.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning trains representations by comparing positive pairs with negative pairs. This paper studies a global objective that compares each positive pair against all negatives associated with an anchor. From an optimization perspective, it explains why methods such as SimCLR need large batches to obtain satisfactory results and seeks to remove that requirement.

The proposed algorithm, SogCLR, is a memory-efficient stochastic method for optimizing this global objective. The analysis shows that its optimization error becomes negligible after sufficiently many iterations under a stated reasonable condition. For a slightly different global contrastive objective, the authors instead establish diminishing optimization error. These are distinct guarantees tied to the objective and conditions analyzed.

On ImageNet-1K self-supervised learning, SogCLR with a batch size of 256 achieves performance similar to SimCLR with a batch size of 8192. This demonstrates that small batches can work well with the proposed optimization approach. The paper also explores applying the technique to other contrastive losses, including two-way losses for bimodal learning.
icml-2022-provable-stochastic-optimizati.tldr: SogCLR optimizes a global contrastive objective and empirically matches large-batch SimCLR performance using much smaller batches.

paragraphs: Image classifiers can overfit when training examples are scarce or unevenly distributed across classes. This paper proposes adding pure random-noise images to training alongside natural images. The noise images are complete training inputs, rather than small perturbations added to existing images, making the proposal a different use of noise from familiar augmentation techniques.

The enabling component is Distribution-Aware Routing Batch Normalization, or DAR-BN. This layer allows one network to train on both natural images and pure noise. The authors report that the resulting training encourages generalization and suppresses overfitting. The method can also be layered on top of existing augmentations without requiring specialized image-generation or training procedures.

Experiments report significant improvements and state-of-the-art results across CIFAR-10-LT, CIFAR-100-LT, ImageNet-LT, Places-LT, and CelebA-5. These results support the usefulness of pure-noise training for the evaluated imbalanced classification problems. The approach matters because the additional training data are simple to generate, and the abstract reports that training remains fast and efficient.
icml-2022-pure-noise-to-the-rescue-of-in.tldr: Training with pure random-noise images through DAR-BN improves generalization and reported performance on multiple imbalanced image-classification datasets.

paragraphs: End-to-end speech translation often relies on pretraining with source-language transcripts, but those transcripts are not always available. This paper investigates how well a system can learn directly from paired speech and translations. It revisits previously useful techniques and assembles practices that favor training a Transformer-based translation system from scratch.

The authors also introduce a parameterized distance penalty to help speech self-attention model local relationships. This supplies an adjustable preference for locality within the attention mechanism. Alongside the training practices, it forms a system designed to learn without transcript-based speech-recognition or text-translation pretraining.

Across four benchmarks covering 23 languages, the system matches or exceeds previous pretrained approaches without using transcripts or pretraining. A gap remains in extremely low-resource settings, so the results do not eliminate the value of pretraining under all data conditions. The paper additionally demonstrates the feasibility of learning acoustic features directly from raw speech with a neural model, reporting encouraging translation results from that direction.
icml-2022-revisiting-end-to-end-speech-t.tldr: Training practices and a learned locality penalty enable competitive speech translation from paired speech and translations alone, though very low-resource gaps remain.

paragraphs: Multiplex network embedding learns representations of nodes in networks with multiple layers. This paper argues that existing approaches overlook structural roles, which provide information about how similarly nodes are positioned within network structure. RMNE incorporates that information so the learned representations preserve structural similarity across the entire multiplex network.

Its central mechanism is a role-modified random walk that generates sequences of nodes. These sequences can include a node’s neighbors within a layer, nodes sharing its structural role, and structural-role members across layers. The representation-learning process therefore receives information about both neighborhood connections and role relationships. A further variant integrates structural roles with an existing collaborative embedding method.

The authors evaluate their methods on network reconstruction, node classification, link prediction, and multi-class edge classification. Across eight public real-world multiplex networks, the methods outperform state-of-the-art baselines in the reported experiments. These results support structural-role information as a useful addition to multiplex representations across several tasks that depend on understanding nodes and their relationships.
icml-2022-role-based-multiplex-network-e.tldr: RMNE uses role-aware random walks to preserve structural similarities across multiplex network layers and improve several network-learning tasks.

paragraphs: Q-learning can become unstable even when its value estimates use simple linear function approximation. Practical systems often add target networks and experience replay, but the separate theoretical contributions of these tools are not fully understood. This paper develops an exploration variant of linear Q-learning and analyzes how its stabilizing components work together.

The algorithm combines a second-order update rule, a collection of target networks, and a mechanism resembling experience replay. A modular analysis identifies the roles of these components. Together, they yield state-of-the-art regret bounds for linear Markov decision processes while retaining memory requirements that do not grow with the number of elapsed learning steps.

The analysis also considers a more permissive notion of approximation error and shows that performance degrades gracefully under it. In addition, the algorithm partially inherits problem-dependent regret bounds involving an effective feature dimension. The contribution connects stability, learning efficiency, and bounded memory within the analyzed setting, while also examining how departures from exact approximation affect performance.
icml-2022-stabilizing-q-learning-with-li.tldr: A stabilized linear Q-learning variant achieves strong regret guarantees with memory independent of elapsed steps and graceful degradation under approximation error.

paragraphs: The paper studies stochastic maximization of continuous objectives with a weak diminishing-returns structure, in both offline and online settings. Its key idea is to optimize a specially constructed auxiliary function F. For the stated smooth, gamma-weakly DR-submodular objectives, every stationary point of F gives a 1 − exp(−gamma) approximation to the original objective’s global maximum.

The offline algorithm uses this auxiliary function to boost gradient ascent. It achieves an approximation factor of 1 − exp(−gamma) − epsilon squared after O(1/epsilon squared) iterations, improving the stated approximation ratio of classical gradient ascent. The construction therefore changes what reaching a stationary point can guarantee about the original maximization problem.

For online learning, the same function supports an algorithm with adversarially delayed stochastic gradient feedback. Its regret is O(square root of D) relative to an approximate hindsight benchmark, where D summarizes feedback delays. Without delay, it obtains O(square root of T) regret with constant gradient queries per step. Numerical experiments also demonstrate the effectiveness of the boosting methods.
icml-2022-stochastic-continuous-submodul.tldr: An auxiliary objective strengthens gradient-based approximation guarantees for stochastic submodular maximization and supports online learning with delayed feedback.

paragraphs: Video understanding requires recognizing how events develop over time, but the authors find that Video Transformers still favor spatial information over temporal dynamics. Their ability to capture long-range dependencies does not by itself ensure that they learn the time-dependent relationships needed for a task. The paper introduces extra self-supervised tasks to address this bias.

One task teaches the model the temporal ordering of video frames and encourages low-confidence outputs when frames are randomly shuffled. This makes frame order part of the learning signal. Another task asks the model to learn the temporal flow direction of video tokens across consecutive frames, strengthening its attention to relationships that unfold through time.

Experiments across video action-recognition tasks demonstrate the method’s effectiveness and compatibility with state-of-the-art Video Transformers. The contribution is a set of additional training signals that directly target temporal understanding. The reported findings support using these signals to reduce reliance on spatial correlations and improve the video representations learned by the evaluated models.
icml-2022-time-is-matter-temporal-self-s.tldr: Frame-order and temporal-flow self-supervision help Video Transformers learn temporal dynamics and improve action-recognition performance.

paragraphs: Visual tracking requires identifying a target and estimating its bounding box. Recent anchor-free Siamese trackers estimate distances to the box’s four sides, but the paper identifies inaccurate localization in complex scenes as a problem. UAST addresses this by giving box estimation a probabilistic representation that can express uncertainty and ambiguity.

For each of the four box offsets, UAST predicts a discretized probability distribution using regression vectors. This represents multiple possible offset values and provides a probabilistic measure of localization uncertainty. The method therefore supplies more information about the box estimate than a single predicted distance for each side.

The authors also introduce a joint prediction head for target classification and localization quality, motivated by the strong relationship between uncertainty and regression accuracy. This aims to support reliable tracking while avoiding inconsistencies between training and inference in how classification and quality are estimated. Experiments on several challenging tracking benchmarks demonstrate the approach’s effectiveness and superiority over other Siamese trackers in the reported evaluation.
icml-2022-uast-uncertainty-aware-siamese.tldr: UAST represents bounding-box offsets as probability distributions and jointly learns classification and localization quality to improve Siamese tracking.

paragraphs: Client-level differential privacy in the federated algorithms considered here involves clipping transmitted model updates before adding privacy noise. Clipping limits the magnitude of an update, but it also changes the information used for learning. This paper studies that effect, emphasizing that clipping client updates differs substantially from clipping gradients in centralized private training.

The authors first show empirically that clipped federated averaging can perform surprisingly well when neural networks are trained on highly heterogeneous client data. They partly explain this through an observation that client updates become similar for several popular deep architectures. Thus, differing local datasets do not necessarily translate into equally disparate updates throughout training.

Building on that observation, the paper analyzes convergence of differentially private FedAvg and relates clipping bias to the distribution of client updates. This connects the practical behavior of clipping to the geometry of the information clients transmit. The contribution combines empirical evidence with theoretical analysis to clarify when clipping can be less damaging than data heterogeneity alone might suggest.
icml-2022-understanding-clipping-for-fed.tldr: An empirical and theoretical study links the effects of clipping in private federated averaging to the distribution of client updates.

paragraphs: A classifier’s confidence should reflect how uncertain its predictions actually are. Strong predictive accuracy does not ensure this calibration. Mixup, which creates training examples through convex combinations of pairs of examples, has empirically improved calibration in many applications. This paper seeks a theoretical explanation of when and how that benefit arises.

The authors analyze natural statistical models and prove calibration improvements from Mixup in high-dimensional settings. Within the analysis, the calibration benefit grows as model capacity increases. Experiments on common architectures and datasets support the theoretical findings. The result ties Mixup’s usefulness to the modeled setting and capacity, rather than asserting an unconditional improvement for every learner.

The paper also examines semi-supervised learning, where incorporating unlabeled examples can sometimes worsen calibration. Adding Mixup mitigates this issue and yields provable calibration improvements in the studied framework. Together, these analyses provide a way to understand how the augmentation affects confidence estimates, including situations where learning from additional unlabeled data creates a calibration problem.
icml-2022-when-and-how-mixup-improves-ca.tldr: Statistical analyses explain Mixup’s calibration benefits in high-dimensional and semi-supervised settings, with supporting experiments.
